• Saturday before Election: Counties, cities and townships must be open from 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m.  
o Exception: For town general elections held in March, the clerk’s office must be open from 10:00 
a.m. to 12 noon. Note: If the county is administering ABs for this election, the county must 
remain open until 3:00 p.m.  
• Before the general election in a state election year, counties, cities and townships must be open from 
9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. 2 Saturdays before Election Day and the Sunday immediately preceding Election 
Day. 
• Day immediately before Election Day: Counties, cities and townships must remain open until 5:00 p.m.  
o Exception: If ‘day immediately before’ is a Saturday or Sunday, counties and municipalities do not 
need to be open until 5:00 p.m.  
Note: There is not a Minnesota Statutes or Rules requirement to publish or post the office’s absentee voting 
hours. However, many offices will do so as a public service best practice.  
  
 
 
Office of the Minnesota 40 City Clerk Election Manual 
Secretary of State                                                
How – Ballots & Ballot Boards 
Anticipating Absentee Voter Counts 
Use your past experience in similar elections and feedback from county and/or municipal election 
administrators to estimate the number of anticipated absentee voters. Adjust for health care facilities within 
your jurisdiction and for municipal growth. Some counties have formulas to use for this process.  
Ballot Supply Has Not Arrived 
Ballots must be available for absentee voters at least 46 days before the election. If the vendor preparing your 
ballot is late in providing them, absentee voting must still begin as scheduled. You must accommodate absentee 
voters under emergency procedures using substitute ballots. (This situation is similar to running out of printed 
ballots at the polling place on Election Day.) Minn. Stat. 204B.35, subd. 4; 204B.39 
Substitute ballots are prepared to look like the official ballots as much as possible. The words “Substitute” must 
be printed in brackets directly above the words “Official Ballot” on the ballots. When delivered, these ballots 
must be accompanied by an initialed affidavit from the election official who prepared them that lists the reason 
why the official ballots were not ready. Minn. Stat. 204B.39 
Issuing Ballots 
An application is required before an absentee ballot can be issued. Any eligible voter may apply for an absentee 
ballot using the Minnesota process. If an applicant is not registered, they will register as part of the absentee 
voting process. Minn. Stat. 203B.02; 203B.04, subds. 1 & 4 
Note: Minnesota law does not provide for a continuous absentee ballot request. A voter who has voted AB for 
an election of the same type in the past must submit a new absentee ballot application form for the current 
election.  
Ballot Boards 
The governing body of the jurisdiction administering regular absentee voting must authorize an absentee ballot 
board by ordinance or resolution. The absentee ballot board is a special board of election judges or election 
administrators that process and count returned regular absentee ballots. The county auditor must establish a 
UOCAVA ballot board to process returned UOCAVA absentees.  
Minnesota law does not provide a defined time period for establishing a ballot board. However, as a regular AB 
board must meet at regular intervals shortly after the receipt of returned absentee ballots and a UOCAVA 
board must meet immediately after ballots are returned, it is good practice to have the board established by the 
start of the elections absentee period. Minn. Stat. 203B.121, subd. 1 
The absentee ballot board must consist of a sufficient number of election judges trained in the handling and 
processing of absentee ballots. The board may include deputy city clerks who have received training on AB 
processing. Election Judges performing ballot board duties must be of different major political parties; deputy 
clerks are exempt from the party balance requirement. Minn. Stat. 203B.121, subd. 1   
Notes:  
A sample resolution establishing a ballot board is available in the Absentee Voting Administration Guide.  
When a city clerk is designated to administer regular absentee voting for county/state/federal elections, the 
designation must specify whether the clerk is responsible for the administration of the ballot board. 
  
 
 
Office of the Minnesota 41 City Clerk Election Manual 
Secretary of State                                                
 Temporary Absentee Voting Locations 
Counties or authorized municipal clerks are now permitted to designate additional temporary locations for 
voting before Election Day. These temporary locations can include different dates and hours than those 
required by Minn. Stat. 203B.085. Additional temporary locations must be designated at least 47 days before 
the election, and notice must be provided to OSS to include the dates, times, and locations.  
County auditors or municipal clerks who are authorized to administer absentee voting may establish temporary 
in-person absentee voting locations. Temporary locations allow for flexibility in scheduling a specific date and 
time that the temporary location will operate, but certain requirements must still be met. 
When Is It Required to Established a Temporary Absentee Voting Location? 
In certain circumstances, a county or municipality may be required to establish a temporary absentee voting 
location upon request from an eligible entity. 
Post-secondary temporary absentee voting locations 
If requested by an eligible post-secondary institution or its student government, a temporary absentee voting 
location must be established for the state general election or odd-year city general election. The requirement 
does not apply for any other elections. 
To be eligible, the post-secondary institution must: 
• Provide on-campus housing to 100 or more students; and 
• Submit a request for the temporary absentee voting location to the county auditor no later than May 31. A 
request is only valid for that specific election (state general election – November of the even year, or the 
city general election in November of the odd year). 
Temporary absentee locations requested by post-secondary institutions must be: 
• Mutually agreed upon between the institution (or student government) and the county auditor 
• Open to the public 
• On campus or within one-half mile and easily accessible to students 
• Established for at least one day 
• Compliant with state and federal laws 
Election officials should work with the institution to ensure that the site meets the requirements above, as well 
as any other administrative or security considerations that provide for safe and accessible voting. See the 
section “Choosing a location” for additional considerations. 
Both parties may also mutually agree upon an alternative site that does not meet all requirements listed above 
(e.g. further than half mile from campus). The institution may withdraw their request at any time by notifying 
the auditor or municipal clerk. 
Funding is also available to reimburse expenses related to established temporary locations at post-secondary 
institutions. See the section “Reimbursement for post-secondary institution absentee locations” for additional 
information. 
 
 
  
 
 
Office of the Minnesota 42 City Clerk Election Manual 
Secretary of State                                                
Designating Temporary Absentee Voting Locations 
Counties or municipalities can set up absentee voting sites in addition to their main location. These locations 
can have different dates and hours than the regularly established schedule. 
Note: for a standalone city, town, or school district election, the school district or municipal clerk takes on 
the role of “county auditor” and is responsible for administering absentee voting, including temporary 
locations, unless the county agrees to perform these duties Minn. Stat. 203B.05. 
• A temporary absentee voting location must be designated at least 47 days before the election. 
• The designation must include the dates, times, and address of the location. 
• The Office of the Secretary of State (OSS) must be notified when the designation is made. 
• Within five business days of designating a temporary polling place, the county or city must post the 
location’s address and voting hours on its official website. 
• The OSS must post any designated locations and their hours on its website within five business days of 
receiving the notice. 
Use of SVRS at Temporary Absentee Voting Locations 
Although SVRS use is not required for temporary locations, it is strongly recommended to assist with ballot 
tracking, cross-county coordination, and balancing procedures. 
Once a site is selected, if the county or city will be using SVRS, the site can be added into SVRS as an additional 
location. 
If a jurisdiction plans to use early voting, they will be required to use SVRS to process applications for voters. 
Choosing a location 
When considering a temporary absentee voting location, a site visit should be conducted in advance to ensure 
the location is suitable and any issues can be addressed before voting begins. 
Discuss and resolve any questions from the site visit with facility contacts for the temporary location. Ensure 
relevant information is captured in a polling place agreement/contract so that all parties understand key details, 
including formal support and coordination from the facility, documentation of any changes, and establishing 
contacts and chain of command for any scenarios in which the staff might need support. 
To assist with evaluating potential temporary absentee voting locations, carefully consider the following: 
Accessibility 
Is the building accessible to voters with disabilities under ADA standards? 
• Review considerations under federal and state laws. 
• Use the Polling Place Accessibility Diagnostic Tool to review polling places for compliance with accessibility 
requirements. 
Facility services 
• Is the lighting, electricity, and ventilation of the space sufficient? 
• Does the space have enough working restrooms for election officials and voters to use? 
• Is water and/or refrigeration available? 
• To support staff working in a space for several hours, as well as a potentially high volume of voters, does the 
space meet the need to support individuals with their basic needs throughout the day? 
 
  
 
 
Office of the Minnesota 43 City Clerk Election Manual 
Secretary of State                                                
Internet 
• If SVRS is being used to administer absentee voting in the temporary location, a secure and authorized 
internet connection is required. 
• Locations in non-government facilities should connect through the county or city's VPN, unless additional 
arrangements have been approved by OSS. Please reach out to the OSS as far in advance as possible to 
coordinate any questions or details related to internet access at a temporary voting location. 
• If SVRS is not being used, it is strongly recommended that the voting location is established in an internet-
connected building so staff can access communication channels needed for facility or community support, 
resources and information from the OSS website that may help in providing voter service, and other 
resources and materials administrators may need to access to support voters in their community. 
Secure handling and storage of voting equipment or materials 
• Each voting location must have adequate space for voting equipment and all materials to be kept safe from 
public access before, during, and after voting takes place. 
• Consider reviewing the CISA Physical Security Checklist for Polling Locations as part of your review and 
preparation for voting at the temporary location. 
Public access plan within the space 
• Will the space be quiet and private, or is it shared with other public events? 
• What will you need to do to secure the voting equipment and materials, ensure constant monitoring of the 
space when the public is present, and consider voters’ needs if there is noise or other distractions in the 
space? 
• Will you need additional materials, such as barriers or stanchions, to properly define and divide the space, as 
necessary? 
• Will the space be adequate to accommodate the anticipated voter traffic? Plan around room for lines to 
form, flow through the location, furniture for election workers and voters, ability to enter and exit without 
trouble or physical barriers, etc. 
• Voter privacy at ballot-marking stations and within the voting area 
• If the location is in a public space or building, will the space be sufficient for voters to be given adequate 
voting privacy at standing and seated voting booths, as well as for those using the assistive voting device? 
• Can voters travel through the voting area with the ability to privately cast their ballots? 
Preparing the Location 
After selecting a location, create a thorough plan to address, at minimum, deployment of equipment and 
materials, proper staffing, and polling place layout that balances voter access with privacy and security. Some 
considerations for your planning should include: 
• Establish contact with the site / facility manager who will be necessary to aid with access, set-up, 
administration, troubleshooting on-site, crowd control and security, etc. 
• Design layout for tables, signage, and voting stations in a way that ensures privacy and a smooth voter flow. 
Consider line management tools, such as stanchions or signage, that can help keep order within the space 
and reduce either confusion or physical obstacles. An assistive voting device must be available for voters to 
use. Place the assistive voting device in an easy-to-access area that is also private to any passersby (ballot 
screen not facing other voters). 
• Plan around lighting, seating, and accessibility considerations to ensure the space is fully compliant with 
voters’ access needs and is a comfortable work environment for staff. 
• Ensure access to enough electrical outlets to power computers, printers, assistive voting device, ballot 
tabulator, etc. 
  
 
 
Office of the Minnesota 44 City Clerk Election Manual 
Secretary of State                                                
• Arrange voting materials needed for each site, such as ballot quantities (or ballot styles printing option, if 
possible), computers, printers, power cords, print materials (applications, envelopes needed, log forms, 
signage, etc.) and voting equipment. Ensure that you have adequate amounts of all materials and a well-
defined transportation plan to securely deliver all items securely to and from the site. 
Important note: a temporary absentee voting location must be prepared to provide all ballot styles for that 
jurisdiction. If the county is administering, all ballot styles in the county must be available. If the city is 
administering, all ballot styles in the city must be available. You should plan for more ballot quantities for the 
precinct(s) closest to the temporary absentee voting location. 
• Secure all voting materials on-site, including ballots and sealed ballot return containers, so they are not left 
unattended or vulnerable. 
• Plan for any ballot drop-offs where a voter wishes to leave their voted mail ballot with staff. 
• Do you have a secure ballot box or a locked room where you can store any ballots dropped off at the 
temporary location? 
• Do you have a copy of the agent return log to record the required information when an agent drops off 
someone else’s ballot? 
• Physical security should mirror Election Day expectations. Temporary absentee voting locations should 
follow the same security standards expected at Election Day polling places: 
• Controlling access to both voting areas and election materials to ensure only authorized individuals are 
present. 
• Protecting equipment, such as laptops or ballot counters, from unauthorized use, tampering, or theft. 
• Monitoring the flow of voters throughout the site to maintain orderly traffic and safeguard voter privacy 
during the voting process. 
• Developing and sharing a clear emergency plan so all staff know who they may contact and when they need 
support throughout the voting process: facility management, security, IT staff, local law enforcement, 
county elections staff, OSS, etc. 
• Plan for any ballot drop-offs where a voter wishes to leave their voted mail ballot with staff. 
• Do you have a secure ballot box or a locked room where you can store any ballots dropped off at the 
temporary location? 
• Do you have a copy of the agent return log to record the required information when an agent drops off 
someone else’s ballot? 
• Consider how you will enforce restrictions on campaigning near absentee locations – within the polling 
place and within 100 feet of the room in which a polling place is situated, to the extent practicable. 
Methods of Administration 
Prior to arranging staff and supplies, plan for: 
• Whether SVRS will be used to administer absentee voting; and 
• If SVRS is being used, whether the site will be using the in-person absentee envelope voting process or 
direct balloting. 
• How ballots will be handled at each temporary site 
When choosing between these methods, consider factors such as the timing of the site (early in the absentee 
period vs. closer to Election Day), available technology, anticipated voter volume, travel needed to and from the 
site to secure voted ballots, and available staff resources and expertise to manage the site(s) for one day or 
more. 
 
  
 
 
Office of the Minnesota 45 City Clerk Election Manual 
Secretary of State                                                
In-person absentee envelope voting 
With this process, voters mark their ballots privately and place them in absentee ballot signature envelopes. 
Election judges or staff complete the witness portion of the signature envelope, and then the envelope is placed 
into a secured storage location. In this method, SVRS use is not required, but strongly encouraged. 
• If SVRS will be used, staff should be trained properly in the use of SVRS for in-person absentee, voting and 
enter voters as “in-person” through the absentee module. 
• Review the SVRS Absentee Voting Training Certification for Designated Users for more information on 
training and certification to administer absentee voting using SVRS. 
• If SVRS will not be used, staff can use a Master List provided by the county to know which voters are 
currently registered and those who will need to complete registration documentation before voting. As 
voters complete the paper absentee application through this process, staff should also keep a record of 
voters casting ballots on a spreadsheet for reconciling statistics. 
• Regardless of whether SVRS is used, administrators must complete detailed statistics reconciliation 
processes to ensure that the number of applications completed equals the number of absentee ballot 
signature envelopes submitted at the temporary location that day. 
Early voting 
Early voting allows voters to mark and cast their ballots on-site using a tabulator or scanner. This approach can 
speed up processing of voters on the front end and the statistics reconciliation on the back end, and also 
eliminates the need for the absentee ballot board to open and process all the envelopes and ballots. However, 
administrators should also consider the additional equipment and testing needed and ensure that there is an 
approved SVRS connection and trained staff to administer the direct balloting process in SVRS. 
Ballot security and chain of custody (CoC) 
Based on the method of absentee voting you choose to administer, ensure the security of ballots and election 
materials at every step. Use sealed, clearly labeled containers to protect ballots during storage and transit. Keep 
a detailed log of all handoffs—recording who handled the materials, when, and where—to maintain an unbroken 
chain of custody. Consider how ballots will be securely transported and stored at the end of the night. Be sure 
to incorporate each temporary location into your overall chain of custody plan so that every site is managed 
with the same level of detail as permanent polling places. 
Staffing and training 
Determining the right number of staff for a temporary absentee voting site starts with understanding your 
expected turnout. Review absentee and Election Day turnout data for the precincts in the area to help with 
predicting the number of voters that may use the temporary location. Factor in any special promotions or 
outreach efforts that could increase participation. 
Once you have estimated site traffic, assign enough trained personnel to manage each stage of the process, 
greeting voters and assisting with registration to handling ballots and overseeing equipment. Ensure every team 
member receives comprehensive training on their specific duties, including: 
• Overall administration of the absentee voting process 
• Proper use of SVRS (if applicable) 
• Chain of custody procedures for ballots and materials 
• Security and privacy protocols 
When in doubt, air on the side of caution and overstaff, or have additional staff available on standby for quick 
deployment. It is easier to scale back than to quickly ramp up. 
  
 
 
Office of the Minnesota 46 City Clerk Election Manual 
Secretary of State                                                
Backup planning 
Unexpected issues can arise. Plan and prepare to have contingency measures in place to minimize the impact of 
any unplanned disruptions: 
Supplies 
Keep extra supplies on hand, including ballots, materials for the envelope process if SVRS is temporarily 
unavailable, pens, stickers, etc. 
Technical fallbacks 
Document clear procedures for internet or equipment failures. Assign a staff member to monitor connectivity, 
have a mobile hotspot available, and train your team on how to switch to manual processes (such as paper-
based check-in or envelope drop-off) until systems are restored. 
Emergency situations 
Consider what you will do if the temporary absentee voting location becomes unusable for some or all the time 
designated due to power failure, flooding, or other emergencies. Is there a suitable location nearby that could 
serve as a backup on short notice (for example, another room in the building or a nearby facility)? Is it possible 
to reschedule for another date and time? 
Reimbursement for temporary absentee locations at post-secondary institutions 
Counties and cities are eligible for reimbursement for administering absentee balloting for post-secondary 
absentee locations. The reimbursement is for temporary polling locations on post-secondary institution 
campuses that provide on-campus student housing to 100 or more students. The deadline to submit 
reimbursement applications is December 15th of each year following the November general election. 
Eligible expenses (Minn. Stat. 203B.0815) 
1. Voting equipment purchasing and programming 
2. Secure storage for voting equipment and supplies 
3. Staff costs for election administrators, election judges, or other election officials 
4. Ballot and voting materials printing 
5. Set-up costs including transportation, parking, and office supplies 
6. Voting booths 
7. Technology necessary to conduct voting at the polling location 
Eligible reimbursements must not exceed 
1. $5,000 for one polling location the first year applying 
2. $3,000 for each additional polling location in the first year 
3. $3,000 for each polling location in subsequent years 
The OSS will circulate more information in advance of the deadline detailing the process to submit a claim to 
reimburse expenses for administering a campus temporary absentee voting location. 
Contact elections.grants.oss@state.mn.us with any questions. 
 
  
 
 
Office of the Minnesota 47 City Clerk Election Manual 
Secretary of State                                                
Election Day  
Voting Hours & Postponement 
For state primaries and general elections, polling places must be open from 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.  
For municipal elections, the minimum voting hours for cities in the metropolitan area are from 10:00 a.m. to 
8:00 p.m. For municipal elections outside the metropolitan area, minimum hours are from 5:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. 
The “metropolitan area” for elections is defined as the counties of Anoka, Carver, Chisago, Dakota, Hennepin, 
Isanti, Ramsey, Scott, Sherburne, Washington and Wright. Minn. Stat. 205.175, subd. 1 
Voters waiting in line at closing time are allowed to register and/or vote. Those who arrive after the closing 
hour cannot vote.  
Local municipal elections not held in conjunction with a state or federal election may be postponed for 
inclement weather. When one or more local jurisdictions are holding elections in conjunction with one another, 
the jurisdiction with the largest local geographic area has the authority, after consulting with other auditors and 
clerks, to postpone the election. A decision to postpone must apply to every precinct in the jurisdiction and 
must be made no later than 6:00 p.m. on the day before the election. A postponed election must be 
rescheduled for the next following Tuesday. An election that is postponed due to weather may be postponed 
again. Minn. Stat. 204C.05; 205.07, subd. 1a; 205.105; 205.175 
Activity in or Near the Polling Place 
Authorized Persons in the Polling Place during Voting 
The polling place will be administered by the head election judge and the other election judges on Election Day. 
No public official, including the clerk may assume the duties of an election judge simply because they hold 
elected or appointed office. All election judges must be eligible to serve, trained, and appointed according to the 
law. Each official on duty in the polling place must wear an identification badge that shows their name and role 
in the election process, such as head judge, election judge, or election judge trainee. The name and role badge 
must not show their party affiliation. Minn. Stat. 204C.06, subd. 2; 204B.19; 204B.20; 204B.21; 204B.25 
During voting hours, the law allows only election judges, people directly engaged in voting, and authorized 
persons to be present in the polling place.  
Authorized persons are: 
• Persons helping a voter who is disabled or unable to read English.  
• Persons who are vouching for a voter’s residence.  
• Observers with written authorization from the OSS, the county auditor, or the clerk for the purpose of 
observing election procedures.  
• Peace officers, if the election judges request their presence to keep order.  
• Children when accompanying voters.  
• Challengers authorized to observe in the polling place.  
• Teachers, elementary and high school students if participating in a mock election that has been 
authorized by the secretary of state.  
• The news media. 
• Persons making a written complaint. Minn. Stat. 204C.06 
 
  
 
 
Office of the Minnesota 48 City Clerk Election Manual 
Secretary of State                                                
Election Materials & Equipment Security 
Election judges represent the first line of defense for the physical and cyber security of Minnesota’s elections. 
All election judges must keep a watchful eye on all voting equipment, removable memory devices, ballots & 
supplies throughout the Election Day. Individuals observed inspecting, assessing or attempting to access or 
connect a device to voting equipment input/output data ports should be addressed by the head judge (and 
additional election judges if needed), with the incident communicated to the local election official immediately. 
Further, it is good practice to view/inspect the seals and any port plugs on voting equipment & ballot storage 
containers throughout the day, with concerns again being reported immediately. 
Voter reports to election judges of observation of any of the above, or of e-mail, text, social media, phone or 
other communications attempting to disrupt or influence the elections process should similarly be reported. 
A sergeant-at-arms or a peace officer may be requested to arrest or remove from the polling place any 
individual who, despite a warning to desist, engages in disorderly conduct, to include attempting to tamper with 
voting equipment. 
A sergeant-at-arms or a peace officer shall not otherwise interfere in any manner with voters. The sergeant-at-
arms or peace officer cannot remain in or within 50 feet of the entrance of the polling place once peace has 
been restored. 
Note the details of all security concerns & how they were addressed on incident log. Minn. Stat. 204C.06, subds. 
5 & 6 
Media Access 
A news media representative may enter a polling place during the voting hours only to observe the voting 
process. A media representative must present photo identification to the head election judge upon arrival at the 
polling place, along with either a recognized media credential or written statement from a local election official 
attesting to the media representative’s credentials.  
A media representative must:  
• Stay at least six feet from voters. 
• Not converse with voters or interfere with the voting process. 
• Not make a list of those voting or not voting. Minn. Stat. 204C.06, subd. 8 
Prohibited Polling Place Activities 
Some persons, items and activities are not allowed in the polling place: 
• Disorderly persons. 
• Intoxicated persons and/or liquor. 
• Persons who are campaigning and/or campaign materials including literature or buttons. 
• Smoking. 
• Lingering. Minn. Stat. 204B.06 
People may not gather or linger in the polling place or within 100 feet of the building in which the polling place 
is located. One exception is an individual conducting an exit poll. Exit polls cannot be conducted within the 
polling place, but may be conducted anywhere outside of the room being used as the polling place. An 
individual conducting an exit poll may only approach voters as they leave the polling place after having voted to 
ask them to take an anonymous written questionnaire. Furthermore, campaigning is also not allowed in the 
polling place, within 100 feet of the building where the polling place is located or on public property if the 
polling place is on public property. This prohibition on campaigning means that campaign buttons, with offices 
  
 
 
Office of the Minnesota 49 City Clerk Election Manual 
Secretary of State                                                
listed on the ballot, cannot be worn in the polling place and campaign signs cannot be displayed within 100 ft of 
the building or on public property if the polling place is on public property. 
Voters, however, may take sample ballots from the newspapers or campaign flyers into the voting booth for 
personal use but they should take care not to display these materials outside of the voting booth. These 
prohibitions also limit where meetings and other activities can be held in polling place sites with multiple rooms. 
Minn. Stat. 204C.06; 204C.13, subd. 2; 211B.11 
See the Election Judge Guide for additional information regarding prohibited conduct in the polling place, at the 
OSS Election Guides webpage (https://www.sos.mn.gov/election-administration-campaigns/election-
administration/election-guides/). 
On Election Day, if the clerk and other elected officials are not eligible to be appointed as election judges (e.g., 
they may be candidates in that election), special care must be taken to ensure that they do not act “in any 
manner” to influence voters in, or near, the polling place.  
Note: Per Schimming v. Riverblood, CAH 7-6347-20326-CV (June 5, 2009), the prohibition of signs and 
campaign materials within 100 feet does not apply to adjacent private property. 
Election Judge Neutrality in the Polling Place 
Even though many judges are affiliated with major parties and often have strong political opinions about 
candidates and ballot questions, once a judge steps into the polling place and takes the oath, they are to remain 
neutral while serving in the role of election judge. Voters have the right to vote in a polling place, free of any 
influence. 
This can be difficult when there is a controversial question on a ballot; especially a constitutional amendment. 
Many people will ask election judges, what does this “mean?” Or, what effect does this or that action have on 
the outcome of the election? 
There should be nothing for election judges to explain orally about any question. The instruction wording is 
printed on the ballot above all questions. The instructions above a constitutional amendment are very clear and 
are explicitly laid out in law. 
It is suggested that when election judges are asked about ballot questions, to refer the voter to the instructions. 
If needed, the election judge may read the instructions out loud. No further explanation is needed. 
Election Judge Code of Conduct 
• Always remain courteous and professional 
• Do not bully or harass local election officials, Head Judges, other election judges, challengers, media, 
election administration representatives, vouchers, voters, or voter assistants 
• Follow all instructions and complete all assignments given to you by the Head Judge 
• Keep the Head Judge informed of all concerns and document details on incident logs 
• Refrain from partisan comments or discussions 
• Do not discuss the decisions and/or actions of political leaders 
• Refrain from personal opinions of current election administration laws, rules, procedures and/or tasks 
• Except to verify party balance, do not disclose or use for any other purpose the party affiliation or 
unaffiliated status of other election judges 
• Avoid any action that may influence how a person votes 
• Respect a voter’s right to use the lawful assistance of any eligible person of their choice 
• Provide respectful assistance to persons with language and/or disability challenges 
• Keep passwords or other access credentials for voting equipment in a safe and secure location. 
 
  
 
 
Office of the Minnesota 50 City Clerk Election Manual 
Secretary of State                                                
• Respect the secret ballot and the privacy of voters: 
o Do not give advice, scrutinize ballots, or reveal how people voted 
o Never disclose personal information about voters found on the  roster; for example, a voter’s birth date. 
o Minn. Stat. 204B.19, subd. 5; 204B.21, subd. 3; 204B.24; 204C.10(e); 204C.15, subd. 1 
Election Day Voter Registration 
Minnesota permits Election Day registration. The clerk may expect 20 percent or more of voters to register at 
the polling places on Election Day. To help avoid delays and congestion, plan a flow of traffic for voter 
registration and voting lines. Consider appointing additional judges to handle registration duties. Judges who 
register voters cannot also handle ballots for the same voter. These duties must be separated. Minn. Stat. 
201.061; 201.018; M.R. 8200.5300 
Election judges must make sure each applicant is registering in the proper place. The clerk must supply an 
accurate precinct finder or precinct map to each polling place in the city. Election judges use the precinct finder 
or precinct map supplied by the clerk to determine if persons are registering in the correct precinct. M.R. 
8200.5300 
The clerk must return the polling place roster(s) and completed VRAs to the county auditor within 48 hours 
following the end of voting. Minn. Stat. 204C.07; 201.018 
Challengers 
Specifically-appointed “challengers” are permitted to be present in the polling place during the hours of voting. 
When challengers arrive at a precinct, they should be directed to the Head Judge to prove their Minnesota 
residency by presenting one of the proofs of residence accepted for Election Day registration (see Minn. Stat. 
201.061, subd. 3 for list) and a letter of appointment from a party or non-partisan candidate. Challengers do not 
need to prove residence in the precinct where they are appointed on Election Day. Minn. Stat. 204C.07; 
204C.12 
The challenger cannot speak to voters. Furthermore, the challenger cannot: 
• Handle or inspect any of the voting materials 
• Make lists of who has or has not voted 
• Compile lists of voters to challenge on the basis of mail sent by a political party that was returned 
undeliverable, and 
• Cannot attempt to influence voting in any manner. 
Challenge of a particular voter’s eligibility to vote takes place through the election judge. The challenger must 
complete the Oath of Challenge to Voters Eligibility form for each challenge and the election judge then 
resolves the issue with the voter. See the Election Judge Guide for more detailed information. 
Appointment as a challenger requires issuance of a written certificate according to the following circumstances: 
• Partisan elections. At an election to fill partisan offices, the chair of an authorized committee of each 
major political party may appoint by written certificate voters from that political party to act as 
challengers of voters at the polling place for each precinct. Only one challenger from each major political 
party for each precinct is allowed to remain in the polling place at one time. 
• Nonpartisan elections. At an election to fill nonpartisan offices, nonpartisan candidates may appoint, by 
written certificate, voters to act as challengers of voters at the polling place for each precinct. Only one 
challenger for each candidate is allowed to remain in the polling place for each precinct at one time. 
• Elections on questions. At an election where a question is to be voted upon, the mayor of a city, or the 
school board of a school district, or the board of supervisors of a town, upon receiving a written petition 
signed by at least 25 eligible voters, must appoint by written certificate one voter for each precinct in 
  
 
 
Office of the Minnesota 51 City Clerk Election Manual 
Secretary of State                                                
the municipality, or school district if applicable, to act as a challenger of voters in the polling place for 
that precinct. 
Emergencies 
County Elections Emergency Plans 
County election officials, in consultation with the political subdivision's local organization for emergency 
management established under Minn. Stat. 12.25 and the municipalities and school districts within the county, 
must develop a county elections emergency plan to be made available for use in all state, county, municipal, and 
school district elections held in that county. 
In developing the county elections emergency plan, the county must address the needs of voters with 
disabilities in all aspects of the plan. 
Where ballot security is affected, the plan must provide procedures to maintain the security of the ballots.  
Emergency Polling Place Relocation Procedures 
When an emergency requires the relocation of the polling place, the plan must include: 
• procedures for securing the ballots and voting equipment 
• notifying the public and other government officials 
• restoring voting activities as soon as possible 
If the county contains jurisdictions that cross county lines, the affected counties must make efforts to ensure 
that the emergency procedures affecting the local jurisdiction are uniform throughout the jurisdiction. 
Local Jurisdiction Elections Emergency Plans 
Cities, towns, and school districts may create a local elections emergency plan that meets the requirements of 
the county elections emergency plan. If a local jurisdiction creates a local elections emergency plan, the 
procedures within the local elections emergency plan govern in all election emergencies within that local 
jurisdiction. 
Review of Election Emergency Plans 
County election officials and any municipality with a local elections emergency plan must review their county or 
local elections emergency plan prior to each state general election. Any revisions to the county or local 
elections emergency plan must be completed and filed with the secretary of state by July 1 prior to the state 
general election. Minn. Stat. 204B.181 
Public Counting 
After all voters in line at 8:00 p.m. have voted, the polling place is open to the public, including members of the 
media and candidates, until votes are counted and results are declared. Please make sure to notify those 
present that the results are only for the poll place itself (do not include absentee ballot totals) and are 
“unofficial.” Election judges will count the ballots/run results tapes, prepare the summary of results, secure and 
turn in election materials. Unless appointed as an election judge, no individual will touch election materials 
during this process, including the clerk. Minn. Stat.204C.19, subd.1; 204C.19, subd. 2; 204C.07  
 
  
 
 
Office of the Minnesota 52 City Clerk Election Manual 
Secretary of State                                                
Summary Statements 
After the last voter in line at 8:00 p.m. has voted, the election judges count the ballots; prepare summary 
statements of the votes for each candidate for each office for and against each ballot question; and sign the 
summary statement. 
Three copies of the summary statements must be completed by the election judges, except that only two copies 
of the summary statements are needed for elections not held on the same day as the state elections. 
In precincts with a precinct ballot counter, the summary statement is printed at the end of the results tape. All 
present election judges must complete the three copies of the summary statement and seal each in individually 
signed envelopes. The first copy must remain attached to the “zeros” report printed when the polls were 
opened.  
Each copy of the summary statements must include the following: 
• Total ballots delivered to your precinct as adjusted by the actual count 
o From any adjustments noted on the incident log; 
• The number of voting booths 
o All stations set up to provide a space for a voter with a ballot; 
• The number of election judges 
o Count number of signatures of judge’s oath; 
• The number of unofficial ballots made, if any; 
• The number of spoiled ballots; 
• The number of duplicate ballots made, if any; 
• The number of unused ballots at the end of the day; 
• The number of persons registered to vote at 7am on Election Day; 
o This number is listed in the back of the pre-registered roster. 
• The number of persons who registered to vote at the polling place on Election Day; 
o This is the number of voter signatures on the Election Day registration roster (or the number of 
EDR voter registration applications). 
• The number of signatures on the rosters (pre-registered roster plus the election day registration roster); 
o This is the number of voter signatures on both rosters. 
• Do not count “AB” notations printed, written, or stamped on the registered roster. Do not count the 
names listed on the non-registered AB supplemental report. 
• The total number of voters that voted at the polling place on Election Day. Minn. Stat. 204C.24
